Text 1
Traditional models of language acquisition have long posited that children's linguistic development follows a predictable sequence of stages. Beginning with simple babbling around 6 months, infants progress through distinct phases: single-word utterances at 12 months, two-word combinations by 18 months, and increasingly complex grammatical structures thereafter. This staged progression culminates in full grammatical competence by age 5, with each phase building systematically upon the previous one.

Text 2
In groundbreaking 2022 research, linguists Kayla Bates and Mugisha Uwimana argue that children's language development is far more dynamic than previously understood. Their longitudinal studies reveal that young learners simultaneously employ multiple linguistic strategies, switching fluidly between simple and complex constructions even within single conversations. The researchers document cases of 15-month-old children producing sophisticated grammatical patterns while still relying on single-word utterances for other communicative functions.
